strengths: Novel two-stage decomposition of fusion objective into interpretable grouping and approximation error components with solid theoretical backing (Theorems 1-2)
First systematic incorporation of neuron importance scores into model fusion with convincing ablation studies demonstrating consistent improvements
Strong experimental results in non-IID and sharded settings where baselines fail (Table 1: 84.5-84.6 vs OTFusion 43.4, vanilla 11.2), addressing an important practical problem in federated learning
Generalizes to arbitrary architectures without task-specific adaptation, unlike prior methods like OTFusion
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple data distribution scenarios with proper statistical rigor (multiple seeds, error bars)
Clear mathematical framework with detailed proofs and honest discussion of limitations in Section 6
weaknesses: Gradient-based variant exhibits concerning practical limitations: hyperparameter sensitive (requires different settings per scenario, Table 5), scales poorly with limited fusion data (38s→632s for 400→6000 samples), and underperforms linear variant on limited data
Unresolved design issue: uses plain MSE instead of weighted MSE because important neurons 'barely change' under weighting, contradicting core motivation for importance scores
Limited experimental scope: only CIFAR-10/100 with VGG11 and ViT; no ImageNet, larger models, or other modalities; knowledge distillation restricted to last layer only
Modest improvements in realistic full-dataset setting with marginal gains over ensemble baseline (Table 3: 72.7 zero-shot vs 75.3 ensemble) and identical performance after fine-tuning
Non-IID experimental design limitations: base models see only 10-20% of data leading to artificially weak baselines; 400 fusion samples from CIFAR-10 may not reflect realistic federated scenarios

Incomplete baseline comparisons: could not benchmark Transformer OTFusion (implementation difficulties), Git Re-Basin marked N/A for 4+ way splits, hyperparameter selection on test scenarios introduces bias
Substantial gap to ensemble remains even in best cases (e.g., 84.5 vs 87.5 in Table 1) raising questions about practical value given ensemble's known alternative of knowledge distillation
Theory-practice gap: strong theory only for linear levels; gradient variant for non-linear levels lacks theoretical justification beyond ad-hoc initialization strategy
20× runtime overhead compared to OTFusion (14.2s vs 0.7s, Table 6) and somewhat incremental contribution combining existing K-means/Hungarian matching with importance weighting

strengths: Clean mathematical formulation with valid decomposition theorem providing interpretable objectives (grouping vs. approximation error)
Generality: works on arbitrary differentiable architectures without architecture-specific adaptation
Comprehensive experimental setup across multiple distribution scenarios (full-dataset, non-IID, sharded) with detailed implementation details
Correct theoretical results with optimality guarantees for linear case and approximation bounds for K-means
Honest acknowledgment of limitations in methodology and practical applicability
weaknesses: Critical methodological flaw: claims to leverage neuron importance scores as main contribution, but abandons weighted MSE loss in practice (Section B.2), using plain MSE instead—directly undermining the core contribution

Experimental validation issues: hyperparameter selection uses test-time data distribution (reports 'best-performing importance score'), baseline methods show unexplained failures (Git Re-Basin 'N/A' entries, implausibly poor OTFusion results)

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 2 guarantees assume linear levels, but experiments use non-linear networks; gradient-based variant (KF Gradient) has no convergence guarantees; (9+ε)-approximation bound is loose with no analysis of practical suboptimality

Limited experimental scope: only CIFAR-10/100, small models (VGG11, ViT), only vision classification; no ImageNet, language models, or heterogeneous architectures; cannot benchmark against Transformer OTFusion due to implementation difficulties

Modest performance gains in practical settings: full-dataset (Table 3) achieves 72.7% vs ensemble 75.3%; non-IID gains come from weak baselines; method consistently underperforms ensemble in all realistic scenarios

Significant computational overhead: 20-100× slower than baselines (Tables 6-7); gradient variant requires 6000 samples vs 400 for linear variants, scaling poorly; unclear if improvements justify costs

Ad-hoc design choices: level partitioning explicitly described as having 'obvious answers' without principled justification; two different hyperparameter configurations for gradient variant without clear selection criteria; squared Euclidean distance motivated only by computational convenience

Incomplete integration of importance scores: Figure 4 shows many neurons have near-zero importance in non-IID settings; limited ablation of importance score benefits; supplementary ablation (Appendix G) is minimal

Incremental novelty: neuron matching (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin), K-means, importance scores, and layer-wise fusion are all established; core claims are decomposition (straightforward application of K-means) and importance score integration (incomplete as noted above)

Weak practical guidance: method requires careful hyperparameter tuning, data-dependent fusion sets, precise level partitioning; unclear when practitioners should prefer this over simple fine-tuning given computational costs

strengths: Clean theoretical framework with rigorous decomposition into grouping and approximation error components (Theorem 1) and meaningful approximation guarantees (Theorem 2)
Novel incorporation of neuron importance scores into model fusion, shown to consistently improve performance and differentiable from prior work
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three distinct training regimes (Non-IID, Sharded, Full-Dataset) with multiple seeds, architectures (VGG11, ViT), and datasets (CIFAR-10/100)
Strong empirical results in non-IID zero-shot fusion, the paper's primary motivation—e.g., 84.5% vs 71.8% (Git Re-Basin) on 4-way VGG11 splits with increasing heterogeneity gains
Elegant generality through composition-levels framework that handles arbitrary architectures without method-specific adaptations, unlike OTFusion for transformers
Insightful analysis including loss/accuracy landscape visualization (Figure 3) demonstrating flatter basins around fused models, and ablation studies on importance scores (Appendix G)
Transparent discussion of limitations including hyperparameter sensitivity and dataset size dependence, demonstrating intellectual honesty
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead (10-100× slower than baselines: KF Linear 78.3s vs OTFusion 0.7s, Tables 6-7) inadequately justified or analyzed; unclear when practitioners should accept this cost versus simpler alternatives

Gradient-based variant exhibits hyperparameter sensitivity, requiring manual selection between two distinct settings (Table 5) without principled decision criteria, undermining practical applicability despite theoretical elegance

Limited experimental scale: only modest models (VGG11, ViT-CIFAR), small datasets (CIFAR-10/100), and maximum 8 fused models; no demonstration on modern large-scale models where fusion is most relevant

Incomplete baseline comparisons: FedMA omitted despite motivation in related work, full KD excluded (overfitting justification insufficiently explained), Transformer OTFusion comparison acknowledged as missing

Importance score selection bias: results report 'best-performing importance score' (Section 5.2) selected from {Uniform, Conductance, DeepLIFT}, introducing oracle selection bias not controlled across comparison methods

Theory-practice gap: approximation error minimization uses unweighted MSE (Section B.2) rather than importance-weighted MSE, justified as practical workaround to prevent noisy neuron inputs rather than principled design
Hyperparameter selection ambiguous: two fusion dataset sizes (400 vs 6000-7000) with unclear selection criteria; Table 1 shows Git Re-Basin and HF as 'N/A' for higher splits without explanation
Missing ablation studies: no systematic analysis of composition-level partitioning choices, relative contribution of grouping vs approximation error, or failure modes where method underperforms

strengths: Addresses real gaps in prior work: reproducibility issues, inflated baselines, and limited non-IID evaluation; zero-shot fusion under distribution shift is practically important for federated learning
Solid theoretical framework with clean decomposition (Theorem 1) into interpretable grouping/approximation errors; Theorem 2 provides optimality (HF) and (9+ε)-approximation (KF) guarantees

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three training regimes (Sharded, Non-IID, Full-Dataset), multiple architectures (VGG, ViT, ResNet), and strong baselines; extensive ablations with proper statistical rigor (std deviations, multiple seeds)
Dramatic empirical improvements in challenging settings where baselines collapse (e.g., 54.4% vs 4.4% on CIFAR-100 ViT sharded 2-way), demonstrating practical value for FL scenarios
Strong reproducibility with open-source code commitment, detailed hyperparameters, complete implementation details, and transparent data partitioning procedures
Honest discussion of limitations: acknowledges hyperparameter sensitivity, data efficiency requirements, computational overhead, and theoretical gaps
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core components (neuron matching, K-means, importance weighting) are established; main contribution is reformulation and retrofitting, which is incremental rather than fundamental

Significant computational overhead (23× slower than OTFusion in some settings) not fully justified; cost-benefit analysis incomplete, especially for full-dataset settings where improvements are modest

Large theory-practice gap: Theorem 2's (9+ε)-approximation bound is very loose; no analysis explaining why empirical K-means solutions achieve near-optimal performance; importance weighting in Theorem 1 lacks theoretical justification

Gradient-based variants require careful tuning despite claims of stable configuration; Authors manually identify hyperparameters across datasets; using plain instead of weighted MSE (Section B.2) appears ad-hoc rather than principled

Non-negligible data requirements for gradient variants (Table 7: 5k vs 1k samples); while augmentation helps, this practical limitation is underexplored and reduces applicability in data-scarce FL settings

Experimental setup concerns: sharded splits with disjoint classes are somewhat artificial; fusion dataset selection varies across experiments; Transformer OTFusion dramatic failures (near-random) lack clear explanation of root cause
Limited scope: no large language model experiments despite claiming generality; missing analysis of when fusion is preferable to alternatives; privacy-utility tradeoffs in FL not examined

Presentation could be clearer: many algorithm variants without guidance on when to use each; connection between theoretical motivation and fixed-previous-levels assumption underexplained; level partitioning heuristic lacks sensitivity analysis

strengths: Clear mathematical decomposition (Theorem 1) with well-motivated representation cost separating clustering and approximation errors
Theoretical guarantees provided: optimality for Hungarian Fusion on linear layers, (9+ε)-approximation for K-means Fusion
Architectural generality—works on VGGs, ResNets, and ViTs unlike prior work limited to specific architectures, through DAG modularity
Strong empirical results in non-IID and sharded data settings, substantially outperforming baselines in challenging zero-shot scenarios
Novel incorporation of neuron importance scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into alignment, improving performance across methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three data regimes, multiple architectures, and datasets with detailed hyperparameter reporting
Open-source promise with extensive supplementary results (hyperparameters, ablations, additional experiments)
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: Hungarian matching used in OTFusion, K-means is standard clustering, importance weighting already in OTFusion; contributions are incremental combinations of existing techniques

Severe computational overhead (15-80× slower than baselines per Tables 10-11) inadequately justified; Section F.5 argument based on full fine-tuning neglects scenarios with shorter fine-tuning budgets

Questionable baseline performance suggesting implementation issues: OTFusion achieves ~1-2% on non-IID splits (random guessing), Git Re-Basin collapse on BloodMNIST; fairness of comparisons unclear (different preactivation conventions noted in footnote)

Gap between theory and practice: Equation (1) defines ideal representation cost, but Algorithm 1 clusters in activation space via K-means, which may not minimize the importance-weighted cost defined theoretically

Contradicts generality claims: 10+ gradient-based hyperparameters (Table 9) despite 'single configuration' claim validated only on similar small-scale image datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet), not ImageNet or other domains

Critical dependency on fusion data size (Table 7): 5k→1k samples causes 17% relative accuracy drop; paper underdiscusses data acquisition, privacy implications, and distribution matching—problematic for stated FL motivation
Mixed results in realistic full-dataset settings: marginal improvements (1.4% in Table 5) at massive computational cost; strongest gains only in artificial non-IID/Sharded scenarios

Artificial experimental setups contradict motivation: states non-IID arises in FL but doesn't evaluate actual FL scenarios, federated methods (FedMA), or iterative training; Dirichlet/sharded partitions don't reflect realistic heterogeneity
Insufficient ablation studies: missing isolation of importance weighting contribution, sensitivity to level granularity, joint vs. sequential optimization, initialization schemes

Theoretical results are incremental: Theorem 1 decomposition lacks deep insight; Theorem 2 directly applies Hungarian algorithm and existing K-means approximation bounds without explaining when/why method succeeds
Generalization scope unclear: all experiments on vision CNNs/ViTs; claims of 'any DAG-modularizable architecture' unsupported for RNNs, LLMs, or non-vision domains
Statistical rigor lacking: standard deviations reported but no significance tests; many differences (1-2 std dev) have unclear practical meaning
Missing critical comparisons: no simple baseline of uniform averaging + identical fine-tuning budget; FedMA and FL variants mentioned but not compared despite FL motivation
Reproducibility gap: promised code URL is missing/incomplete; some training details scattered across appendix; no provision for reproducing exact baseline results
Underdeveloped application (ResNet compression, Table 8): only 5k samples; weak KD baseline unexplained; missing compression method comparisons

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing three concrete gaps in prior work: reproducibility, base model quality, and heterogeneous data evaluation
Strong theoretical foundation with Theorem 1's elegant decomposition into interpretable grouping and approximation errors, and Theorem 2's appropriate approximation guarantees
Novel incorporation of neuron importance scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into model fusion with convincing ablations demonstrating consistent benefits

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (VGG, ResNet, ViT), datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1k, BloodMNIST), and training regimes (sharded, non-IID, full-dataset)
Dramatic improvements in challenging zero-shot non-IID scenarios where prior methods collapse (e.g., 54.5% vs 2.3% for Transformer OTFusion on ViT CIFAR-100)
Flexible framework supporting multiple algorithmic variants (HF/KF, Linear/Gradient), variable model sizes, and >2 models
Excellent reproducibility: open-source implementation, detailed hyperparameters, extensive appendix, implementation details enabling replication
Honest and thorough limitations discussion, proper experimental design with multiple seeds, and insightful visualizations (especially Figure 3 on clustering behavior)
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead: gradient-based methods 20-100× slower than baselines (16.5s vs 0.7s for OTFusion), limiting practical adoption; while Table 12 contextualizes this for fine-tuning scenarios, overhead remains substantial for zero-shot applications

Data-dependent performance: gradient-based variants show substantial degradation with smaller fusion datasets (76.1% → 73.2% with 1k samples), somewhat undermining the 'zero-shot' framing when high-quality fusion data is unavailable

Hyperparameter sensitivity despite claims of stability: gradient-based variants require careful tuning, linear variants need different regularization across problem types (λ=10^-3 vs 10), and automated selection remains future work

Limited methodological novelty: Hungarian matching and K-means are standard algorithms; while the representation-matching framing is elegant, the core contribution is somewhat incremental over activation-based alignment in prior work

Incomplete experimental comparisons: Git Re-Basin limited to pairwise fusion (preventing 4-way/6-way comparison in Table 2), ZipIt! only compared on ImageNet-1k, Transformer OTFusion handicapped by memory constraints (200 samples vs 5000)
Design choices under-justified: level partitioning acknowledged as design choice with no principled guidance, choice of plain MSE over weighted MSE in gradient phase is pragmatic but ad-hoc
Limited analysis of failure modes and heterogeneity effects: paper demonstrates results but provides limited intuition for why methods succeed/fail under different heterogeneity conditions
Missing LLM experiments despite ICML 2026 context and growing importance of large language model merging; noted as future work but weakens contribution
No statistical significance testing despite some differences appearing small relative to variance; unclear whether all reported improvements are meaningful
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to computer vision tasks; applicability to other domains unclear
